t: 3785. Minimum Swaps to Avoid Forbidden Values
o: We may swap any two entries of nums; minimize swaps so nums[i] != forbidden[i] everywhere, or -1. Any target arrangement is a permutation, and the minimum swaps to realize it is (number of misplaced elements) - (number of cycles saved), so we should fix as many conflicts as possible per swap. A single swap fixes two conflicting positions iff their forbidden values differ (they simply exchange values). Conflicts sharing the same forbidden value v must each trade with a 'free' (non-conflicting) position j where neither nums[j] nor forbidden[j] equals v. Example 2: all four positions conflict with forbidden counts 4:1, 6:1, 5:2; two cross-value pairs fix everything in 2 swaps. Example 3 fails feasibility because value 7 is forbidden somewhere but scarce.
k: Minimum swaps = (#conflicts) - (max number of cross-value conflict pairs), where maxPairs = min(S/2, S - maxGroupSize).
Two conflicts with different forbidden values can always be fixed by one mutual swap.
Leftover conflicts (all of one value v) each need a distinct free partner with nums[j] != v and forbidden[j] != v.
Feasibility (Hall-type): for every value v, #(positions forbidding v) <= n - #(occurrences of v in nums), else return -1.

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy pairing with feasibility checks
a.i: Count conflicts grouped by forbidden value; pair groups against each other as much as possible (leaving singles only in the largest group), then match singles to compatible free positions. If any check fails, no amount of swapping works.
s: Collect conflicting indices; if none, return 0.
Hall check: for each value v, count of positions with forbidden = v must be <= n minus count of v in nums; otherwise return -1.
pairs = min(S // 2, S - maxGroup); singles = S - 2*pairs, all of the max-group value v*.
Count free positions with nums != v* and forbidden != v*; if fewer than singles, return -1; otherwise return S - pairs.
a.t: O(n) - a constant number of counting passes over the arrays
a.sp: O(n) for the hash maps of value counts

w: Frame it as permutation-cycle accounting first ('misplaced minus saved cycles'), then derive the pairing rule. Pitfalls: missing the Hall feasibility check (example 3), forgetting BOTH nums[j] != v and forbidden[j] != v for free partners, and assuming one swap can fix two conflicts with the same forbidden value (it cannot). Follow-up: return a concrete swap schedule, or allow one 'overwrite' operation.
